title: Neanderthals in Our Genes
paragraphs: For a long time, people imagined Neanderthals as slow and clumsy cousins who simply lost a competition with modern humans. Genetics has made that picture much harder to defend. When researchers compared the DNA of living people with a Neanderthal genome, they discovered that many of the people they tested carry small pieces of it. In the genomes studied, people whose ancestors lived outside Africa typically carry between one and two percent Neanderthal DNA.

This means that the two groups met and had children together, probably more than once. A study published in two thousand twenty also found small amounts of Neanderthal DNA in African populations, and its authors argued that some of it may have travelled back to Africa with early modern humans. However, the team studied only a limited number of African populations, so the results may not apply to everyone.

None of this proves that every meeting was peaceful, or that the two groups understood each other. It shows only that the boundary between them and us was thinner than once believed. In that sense, a Neanderthal is not a distant relative displayed in a museum. It may be a small part of who we are.
